cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Christ, in a green mandorla, strides toward the great barred doors of a fiery underworld, while figures within the flames reach out. The verse written below — 'Lift up your gates, O ye princes … and the King of glory shall come in' — was read as a prophecy of Christ's descent into hell after his death.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:objects-weimar-liuthard-group-book-c.summary: At the top of this tall plaque Christ ascends in a mandorla toward the hand of God that reaches down from the clouds, flanked by angels. Beneath, the apostles look up in amazement around a central haloed figure with raised arms, and in the lowest register a crowd gathers before a gabled building within city walls. The swirling, agitated figures are typical of the Liuthard Group, the ivory carvers of Charles the Bald's court.
facts: The museum label attributes the cover to the Liuthard Group, named after the scribe Liuthard who worked for Charles the Bald, in the second half of the 9th century.
cur:objects-weimar-liuthard-group-book-c.notes: The subject of the lowest register could not be identified with confidence from the photograph.

cur:objects-essen-senkschmelz-cross.summary: Instead of a sculpted corpus, this jewelled cross carries five large enamel plaques; the central one shows the Crucifixion, with Christ on the cross between the Virgin and St John, while the enamels at the ends of the arms show the evangelist symbols. The intense blues, greens and whites of the enamel glow amid the gold and gems. It is counted among the masterpieces of Ottonian goldsmiths' work.
facts: Its name refers to its five unusually large plaques of senkschmelz ('sunk') enamel, in which the enamel sits in recesses surrounded by plain gold; the border also held 24 small enamels, 21 of which survive.
Its block-shaped arm ends resemble the cubic capitals popular in architecture around the year 1000.

walters:48.2086.11.summary: This reassembled glazed tile shows, within a circle bordered by a diamond pattern, the frontal bust of the Virgin in a dark mantle marked with crosses at the shoulders, with the letters ΘΥ ('of God') of her title at the right. Her head is lost, and at her breast only a damaged golden roundel remains where the Christ Child may once have appeared. The tile belongs to a group the Walters has arranged to suggest a Byzantine icon screen.
facts: The Walters explains that the tiles are related to others from Constantinople and are displayed together to evoke an iconostasis, the screen that separated the sanctuary from the rest of the church.
The museum notes that around the year 1000 such screens bore images of Christ, the Virgin, John the Baptist and other saints.
walters:48.2086.11.notes: Titled 'Virgin and Child' by the museum, but the Child cannot be made out in the damaged tile; possibly he was shown in the roundel on her breast. Image viewed on the Walters image server.

walters:W.42.30R.summary: Within a blue initial D on a gold ground, the crowned King David stands at the left and points to his eyes, while Christ, haloed and robed in red and blue, stands facing him at the right. The initial opens Psalm 26 in the Latin numbering, 'Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea' ('The Lord is my light and my salvation'), and David's gesture shows that it is Christ who gives him sight. Red and blue penwork flourishes frame the text.
facts: The opening words of the psalm, 'Dominus illuminatio mea', are legible beside the initial, followed by 'Dominus protector vite mee a quo trepidabo'.
In illuminated psalters, historiated initials marked the beginnings of the major divisions of the Psalms; Psalm 26 (Latin numbering) began one of these divisions.
The psalter was made for Jernoul de Camphaing, named in a red inscription on fol. 226r.
walters:W.42.30R.notes: Museum date 1250–1275; the 8th-century date in our data was an import error.
